claim: The entorhinal cortex (EC) connects to the hippocampus sending different information from cortical areas that is first processed at the dentate gyrus (DG) including spatial, limbic and sensory information.
source: The entorhinal cortex (EC) connects to the hippocampus sending different information from cortical areas that is first processed at the dentate gyrus (DG) including spatial, limbic and sensory information.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the anatomical and functional organization of the EC-hippocampus connection.

claim: Excitatory afferents from lateral (LPP) and medial (MPP) perforant pathways of the EC connecting to granule cells of the DG play a role in memory encoding and information processing.
source: Excitatory afferents from lateral (LPP) and medial (MPP) perforant pathways of the EC connecting to granule cells of the DG play a role in memory encoding and information processing and are deeply affected in humans suffering Alzheimer's disease and temporal lobe epilepsy, contributing to the dysfunctions found in these pathologies.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the functional role of these pathways.

claim: Excitatory afferents from LPP and MPP are deeply affected in humans suffering Alzheimer's disease and temporal lobe epilepsy, contributing to the dysfunctions found in these pathologies.
source: Excitatory afferents from lateral (LPP) and medial (MPP) perforant pathways of the EC connecting to granule cells of the DG play a role in memory encoding and information processing and are deeply affected in humans suffering Alzheimer's disease and temporal lobe epilepsy, contributing to the dysfunctions found in these pathologies.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about pathological changes in these pathways.

claim: A post-before-pre pairing protocol induced robust t-LTD at LPP-GC synapses (63 ± 5 %, n=14).
source: A post-before-pre pairing protocol induced robust t-LTD at both LPP-GC (63 ± 5 %, n=14: Figure 1b and c) and MPP-GC synapses (59 ± 5 %, n=14: Figure 1l and m), while unpaired control pathways remained unaffected (103 ± 4% and 105 ± 7%, respectively: Figure 1b, c, l and m).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1b and c.

claim: A post-before-pre pairing protocol induced robust t-LTD at MPP-GC synapses (59 ± 5 %, n=14).

evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1l and m.

claim: Unpaired control pathways remained unaffected during t-LTD induction at LPP-GC synapses (103 ± 4%).

claim: Unpaired control pathways remained unaffected during t-LTD induction at MPP-GC synapses (105 ± 7%).

evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1b, c, l and m.

claim: t-LTD was not affected at LPP-GC and MPP-GC synapses in the presence of GABAA and GABAB receptor blockers.
source: In these experimental conditions, t-LTD was not affected at these synapses, indicating that these receptors are not necessary for t-LTD induction (LPP-GC: Control t-LTD: 67 ± 6%, n=6; Bicuculline + SCH50911: 69 ± 11%, n=6; Figure 1—figure supplement 1). MPP-GC synapses: Control t-LTD: 65 ± 8%, n=6; Bicuculline + SCH50911: 75 ± 9%, n=6; Figure 1—figure supplement 1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: GABAA and GABAB receptors are not necessary for t-LTD induction at LPP-GC and MPP-GC synapses.
source: In these experimental conditions, t-LTD was not affected at these synapses, indicating that these receptors are not necessary for t-LTD induction (LPP-GC: Control t-LTD: 67 ± 6%, n=6; Bicuculline + SCH50911: 69 ± 11%, n=6; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing no effect of GABA receptor blockers on t-LTD.

claim: The number of failures increased after t-LTD at LPP-GC synapses (from 43 ± 7% at baseline to 76 ± 6% after t-LTD, n=8).
source: We analysed these and found that the number of failures increased consistently after t-LTD at both LPP-GC (from 43 ± 7% at baseline to 76 ± 6% after t-LTD, n=8: Figure 1d) and MPP-GC synapses (from 40 ± 5% at baseline to 59 ± 4% after t-LTD, n=6: Figure 1n), suggesting a presynaptic mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The number of failures increased after t-LTD at MPP-GC synapses (from 40 ± 5% at baseline to 59 ± 4% after t-LTD, n=6).
source: We analysed these and found that the number of failures increased consistently after t-LTD at both LPP-GC (from 43 ± 7% at baseline to 76 ± 6% after t-LTD, n=8: Figure 1d) and MPP-GC synapses (from 40 ± 5% at baseline to 59 ± 4% after t-LTD, n=6: Figure 1n), suggesting a presynaptic mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1n.

claim: The increase in failures after t-LTD suggests a presynaptic mechanism.
source: We analysed these and found that the number of failures increased consistently after t-LTD at both LPP-GC (from 43 ± 7% at baseline to 76 ± 6% after t-LTD, n=8: Figure 1d) and MPP-GC synapses (from 40 ± 5% at baseline to 59 ± 4% after t-LTD, n=6: Figure 1n), suggesting a presynaptic mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observation of increased failures, which is consistent with presynaptic changes.

claim: PPR increased significantly after t-LTD at LPP-GC synapses (from 1.16±0.11 at baseline to 1.67±0.19 after t-LTD, n=14).
source: We then analysed the PPR at baseline and 30 min after the pairing protocol, identifying a significant increase in the PPR after t-LTD at both LPP-GC (from 1.16±0.11 at baseline to 1.67±0.19 after t-LTD, n=14: Figure 1e) and MPP-GC synapses (from 1.17±0.11 at baseline to 1.81 ± 0.15% after t-LTD, n=14: Figure 1o), again suggesting a presynaptic expression of these two forms of t-LTD.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1e.

claim: PPR increased significantly after t-LTD at MPP-GC synapses (from 1.17±0.11 at baseline to 1.81 ± 0.15% after t-LTD, n=14).

claim: A plot of CV–2 versus the change in the mean evoked EPSP slope mainly yielded points below the diagonal line at LPP-GC synapses (Mean = 0.607 ± 0.054 vs 1/CV2=0.439 ± 0.096, R2=0.337; n=14).
source: A plot of CV–2 versus the change in the mean evoked EPSP slope (M) before and after t-LTD mainly yielded points below the diagonal line at LPP-GC and MPP-GC synapses (LPP-GC: Mean = 0.607 ± 0.054 vs 1/CV2=0.439 ± 0.096, R2=0.337; n=14) and MPP-GC (Mean = 0.596 ± 0.056 vs 1/CV2=0.461 ± 0.090, R2=0.168; n=13).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1f.

claim: A plot of CV–2 versus the change in the mean evoked EPSP slope mainly yielded points below the diagonal line at MPP-GC synapses (Mean = 0.596 ± 0.056 vs 1/CV2=0.461 ± 0.090, R2=0.168; n=13).
source: A plot of CV–2 versus the change in the mean evoked EPSP slope (M) before and after t-LTD mainly yielded points below the diagonal line at LPP-GC and MPP-GC synapses (LPP-GC: Mean = 0.607 ± 0.054 vs 1/CV2=0.439 ± 0.096, R2=0.337; n=14) and MPP-GC (Mean = 0.596 ± 0.056 vs 1/CV2=0.461 ± 0.090, R2=0.168; n=13).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1p.

claim: The CV analysis is consistent with a modification of the release parameters.
source: Figure 1f and p, consistent with a modification of the release parameters (Rodríguez-Moreno and Paulsen, 2008; see Brock et al., 2020 for review).
evidence: This is inferred from the CV analysis data and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The frequency of mEPSPs decreased at LPP-GC synapses after t-LTD induction (baseline 1.4±0.13 Hz, after t-LTD induction 0.7±0.09 Hz, n=6).
source: Under these conditions, a t-LTD similar to previous experiments was evident at both types of synapse (LPP-GC synapses 55 ± 11%, n=6; MPP-GC synapses 67 ± 8%, n=7), and we found that the frequency of mEPSPs decreased at both types of synapse after t-LTD induction: LPP-GC - baseline 1.4±0.13 Hz, after t-LTD induction 0.7±0.09 Hz, n=6 (Figure 1g and h); and MPP-GC - baseline 1.2±0.1 H, after t-LTD induction 0.7±0.07 Hz, n=8 (Figure 1q and r).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1g and h.

claim: The frequency of mEPSPs decreased at MPP-GC synapses after t-LTD induction (baseline 1.2±0.1 Hz, after t-LTD induction 0.7±0.07 Hz, n=8).
source: Under these conditions, a t-LTD similar to previous experiments was evident at both types of synapse (LPP-GC synapses 55 ± 11%, n=6; MPP-GC synapses 67 ± 8%, n=7), and we found that the frequency of mEPSPs decreased at both types of synapse after t-LTD induction: LPP-GC - baseline 1.4±0.13 Hz, after t-LTD induction 0.7±0.09 Hz, n=6 (Figure 1g and h); and MPP-GC - baseline 1.2±0.1 H, after t-LTD induction 0.7±0.07 Hz, n=8 (Figure 1q and r).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1q and r.

claim: No effect on mEPSP amplitude was evident at LPP-GC synapses (baseline 1.13±0.09, after t-LTD 1.13±0.02 mV, n=5).
source: No effect on mEPSP amplitude was evident at any of these synapses: LPP-GC - baseline 1.13±0.09, after t-LTD 1.13±0.02 mV, n=5 (Figure 1i and j); MPP-GC - baseline 1.03±0.07, after t-LTD 1.00±0.09 mV, n=6 (Figure 1s, t).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1i and j.

claim: No effect on mEPSP amplitude was evident at MPP-GC synapses (baseline 1.03±0.07, after t-LTD 1.00±0.09 mV, n=6).
source: No effect on mEPSP amplitude was evident at any of these synapses: LPP-GC - baseline 1.13±0.09, after t-LTD 1.13±0.02 mV, n=5 (Figure 1i and j); MPP-GC - baseline 1.03±0.07, after t-LTD 1.00±0.09 mV, n=6 (Figure 1s, t).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1s, t.

claim: The results are consistent with a decrease in the probability of neurotransmitter release and indicative of a presynaptic locus for these two forms of t-LTD at both types of synapse.
source: Hence, together these results are consistent with a decrease in the probability of neurotransmitter release and they are indicative of a presynaptic locus for these two forms of t-LTD at both types of synapse.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple experimental observations including failure rate, PPR, CV analysis, and mEPSP frequency changes.

claim: t-LTD at LPP-GC synapses was not affected by D-AP5 (66 ± 4%, n=8).
source: In these experimental conditions, t-LTD at LPP-GC synapses was not affected by these antagonists (D-AP5 66 ± 4%, n=8; MK-801 62 ± 9%, n=6; interleaved controls 60 ± 6%, n=8: Figure 2a and b), whereas t-LTD at MPP-GC synapses was blocked in slices treated with either D-AP5 (90 ± 7 %, n=10) or MK-801 (107 ± 10 %, n=6) relative to the interleaved controls (60 ± 7 %, n=8: Figure 2e and f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2a and b.

claim: t-LTD at LPP-GC synapses was not affected by MK-801 (62 ± 9%, n=6).
source: In these experimental conditions, t-LTD at LPP-GC synapses was not affected by these antagonists (D-AP5 66 ± 4%, n=8; MK-801 62 ± 9%, n=6; interleaved controls 60 ± 6%, n=8: Figure 2a and b), whereas t-LTD at MPP-GC synapses was blocked in slices treated with either D-AP5 (90 ± 7 %, n=10) or MK-801 (107 ± 10 %, n=6) relative to the interleaved controls (60 ± 7 %, n=8: Figure 2e and f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2a and b.

claim: t-LTD at MPP-GC synapses was blocked in slices treated with D-AP5 (90 ± 7 %, n=10).
source: In these experimental conditions, t-LTD at LPP-GC synapses was not affected by these antagonists (D-AP5 66 ± 4%, n=8; MK-801 62 ± 9%, n=6; interleaved controls 60 ± 6%, n=8: Figure 2a and b), whereas t-LTD at MPP-GC synapses was blocked in slices treated with either D-AP5 (90 ± 7 %, n=10) or MK-801 (107 ± 10 %, n=6) relative to the interleaved controls (60 ± 7 %, n=8: Figure 2e and f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2e and f.

claim: t-LTD at MPP-GC synapses was blocked in slices treated with MK-801 in the bath (107 ± 10 %, n=6).
source: In these experimental conditions, t-LTD at LPP-GC synapses was not affected by these antagonists (D-AP5 66 ± 4%, n=8; MK-801 62 ± 9%, n=6; interleaved controls 60 ± 6%, n=8: Figure 2a and b), whereas t-LTD at MPP-GC synapses was blocked in slices treated with either D-AP5 (90 ± 7 %, n=10) or MK-801 (107 ± 10 %, n=6) relative to the interleaved controls (60 ± 7 %, n=8: Figure 2e and f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2e and f.

claim: t-LTD at MPP-GC synapses was not affected when MK-801 was loaded into the postsynaptic cell (54 ± 7 %, n=9).
source: When the experiment was repeated by loading the postsynaptic cell with MK-801 (500 µM-1 mM), t-LTD at MPP-GC synapses was not affected (54 ± 7 %, n=9) relative to the interleaved controls (60 ± 7 %, n=8: Figure 2e and f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2e and f.

claim: While t-LTD at MPP-GC synapses requires NMDARs, t-LTD at LPP-GC synapses does not.
source: These results indicate that while t-LTD at MPP-GC synapses requires NMDARs, t-LTD at LPP-GC synapses does not.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of NMDAR antagonists on t-LTD at the two types of synapses.

claim: The NMDARs required for t-LTD at MPP-GC synapses are ionotropic and non-postsynaptic.
source: Moreover, the NMDARs required for t-LTD at MPP-GC synapses are ionotropic and non-postsynaptic, consistent with data from neocortical synapses where presynaptic NMDARs are required for t-LTD (Sjöström et al., 2003; Bender et al., 2006; Nevian and Sakmann, 2006; Rodríguez-Moreno and Paulsen, 2008).
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of bath-applied vs. postsynaptically-loaded MK-801, and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: t-LTD at MPP-GC synapses was completely blocked in slices exposed to Zn2+ (300 nM) (95 ± 5 %, n=7).
source: To determine the subunit composition of the NMDARs involved in t-LTD at MPP-GC synapses, we first repeated the experiments in slices treated with Zn2+ (300 nM), an antagonist of NMDARs containing GluN2A subunits (Bidoret et al., 2009; Andrade-Talavera et al., 2016; Prius-Mengual et al., 2019) that prevented t-LTD (95 ± 5 %, n=7: Figure 2g and h).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2g and h, and citations to previous work on Zn2+ as a GluN2A antagonist.

claim: Ro25-6981 did not affect t-LTD at MPP-GC synapses (55 ± 11 %, n=6).
source: We also repeated the experiments on slices in the presence of Ro25-6981 (0.5 µM), an antagonist of NMDARs containing GluN2B subunits (Hu et al., 2009; Mareš et al., 2021). This antagonist did not affect t-LTD (55 ± 11 %, n=6: Figure 2g and h) and neither did an additional antagonist of NMDARs containing GluN2B subunits, ifenprodil (3 µM, 62 ± 11%, n=6: Figure 2g and h).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2g and h, and citations to previous work on Ro25-6981 as a GluN2B antagonist.

claim: Ifenprodil did not affect t-LTD at MPP-GC synapses (62 ± 11%, n=6).
source: We also repeated the experiments on slices in the presence of Ro25-6981 (0.5 µM), an antagonist of NMDARs containing GluN2B subunits (Hu et al., 2009; Mareš et al., 2021). This antagonist did not affect t-LTD (55 ± 11 %, n=6: Figure 2g and h) and neither did an additional antagonist of NMDARs containing GluN2B subunits, ifenprodil (3 µM, 62 ± 11%, n=6: Figure 2g and h).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2g and h.

claim: PPDA did not affect t-LTD at MPP-GC synapses (61 ± 7%, n=6).
source: Finally, t-LTD was not affected in the presence of PPDA 10 µM, 61 ± 7%, n=6: Figure 2g and h, relative to the pooled interleaved controls (63 ± 6 %, n=9), an antagonist of NMDARs that contain GluN2C/2D subunits (Chen et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2g and h, and citations to previous work on PPDA as a GluN2C/2D antagonist.

claim: The presynaptic NMDARs involved in t-LTD induction at MPP-GC synapses probably contain GluN1/GluN2A subunits.
source: These results indicate that the presynaptic NMDARs involved in t-LTD induction at MPP-GC synapses probably contain GluN1/GluN2A subunits.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of subunit-specific NMDAR antagonists.

claim: Exposure to the broad-spectrum mGluR antagonist LY341495 (100 µM) completely blocked t-LTD at LPP-GC synapses (100 ± 10 %, n=8).
source: Exposure to the broad-spectrum mGluR antagonist LY341495 (100 µM) completely blocked t-LTD at both LPP-GC (100 ± 10 %, n=8: Figure 2c and d) and MPP-GC synapses (99 ± 9 %, n=10: Figure 2i and j).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2c and d.

claim: Exposure to the broad-spectrum mGluR antagonist LY341495 (100 µM) completely blocked t-LTD at MPP-GC synapses (99 ± 9 %, n=10).
source: Exposure to the broad-spectrum mGluR antagonist LY341495 (100 µM) completely blocked t-LTD at both LPP-GC (100 ± 10 %, n=8: Figure 2c and d) and MPP-GC synapses (99 ± 9 %, n=10: Figure 2i and j).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2i and j.

claim: The mGluR5 antagonist MPEP (20 µM) prevented t-LTD at LPP-GC synapses (103 ± 10 %, n=8).
source: Indeed, the mGluR5 antagonist MPEP (20 µM) prevented t-LTD at LPP-GC (103 ± 10 %, n=8: Figure 2c and d) but not at MPP-GC synapses (61 ± 7 %, n=6: Figure 2i and j), whereas the specific mGluR1 antagonist LY367385 (100 µM) did not affect t-LTD at LPP-GC synapses (76 ± 3 %, n=6: Figure 2c and d) but it did block t-LTD at MPP-GC synapses (95 ± 7 %, n=7: Figure 2i and j) relative to their respective interleaved controls (LPP-GC synapses 68 ± 7%, n=9; MPP-GC synapses 65 ± 7%, n=9: Figure 2c, d, i and j).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2c and d.

claim: The mGluR5 antagonist MPEP (20 µM) did not prevent t-LTD at MPP-GC synapses (61 ± 7 %, n=6).
source: Indeed, the mGluR5 antagonist MPEP (20 µM) prevented t-LTD at LPP-GC (103 ± 10 %, n=8: Figure 2c and d) but not at MPP-GC synapses (61 ± 7 %, n=6: Figure 2i and j), whereas the specific mGluR1 antagonist LY367385 (100 µM) did not affect t-LTD at LPP-GC synapses (76 ± 3 %, n=6: Figure 2c and d) but it did block t-LTD at MPP-GC synapses (95 ± 7 %, n=7: Figure 2i and j) relative to their respective interleaved controls (LPP-GC synapses 68 ± 7%, n=9; MPP-GC synapses 65 ± 7%, n=9: Figure 2c, d, i and j).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2i and j.

claim: The specific mGluR1 antagonist LY367385 (100 µM) did not affect t-LTD at LPP-GC synapses (76 ± 3 %, n=6).
source: Indeed, the mGluR5 antagonist MPEP (20 µM) prevented t-LTD at LPP-GC (103 ± 10 %, n=8: Figure 2c and d) but not at MPP-GC synapses (61 ± 7 %, n=6: Figure 2i and j), whereas the specific mGluR1 antagonist LY367385 (100 µM) did not affect t-LTD at LPP-GC synapses (76 ± 3 %, n=6: Figure 2c and d) but it did block t-LTD at MPP-GC synapses (95 ± 7 %, n=7: Figure 2i and j) relative to their respective interleaved controls (LPP-GC synapses 68 ± 7%, n=9; MPP-GC synapses 65 ± 7%, n=9: Figure 2c, d, i and j).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2c and d.

claim: The specific mGluR1 antagonist LY367385 (100 µM) blocked t-LTD at MPP-GC synapses (95 ± 7 %, n=7).
source: Indeed, the mGluR5 antagonist MPEP (20 µM) prevented t-LTD at LPP-GC (103 ± 10 %, n=8: Figure 2c and d) but not at MPP-GC synapses (61 ± 7 %, n=6: Figure 2i and j), whereas the specific mGluR1 antagonist LY367385 (100 µM) did not affect t-LTD at LPP-GC synapses (76 ± 3 %, n=6: Figure 2c and d) but it did block t-LTD at MPP-GC synapses (95 ± 7 %, n=7: Figure 2i and j) relative to their respective interleaved controls (LPP-GC synapses 68 ± 7%, n=9; MPP-GC synapses 65 ± 7%, n=9: Figure 2c, d, i and j).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2i and j.

claim: Both LPP-GC and MPP-GC synapses require mGluR activity to induce these presynaptic forms of t-LTD, but whereas t-LTD at LPP-GC synapses requires mGluR5, mGluR1 receptors are required at MPP-GC synapses.
source: Hence, both LPP-GC and MPP-GC synapses require mGluR activity to induce these presynaptic forms of t-LTD, but whereas t-LTD at LPP-GC synapses requires mGluR5, mGluR1 receptors are required at MPP-GC synapses.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of mGluR subtype-specific antagonists on t-LTD at the two types of synapses.

claim: The L-type Ca2+ channel blocker nimodipine (10 µM) did not impede t-LTD induction at LPP-GC synapses (79 ± 4 %, n=6).
source: This channel blocker did not impede t-LTD induction at LPP-GC (79 ± 4 %, n=6: Figure 3a and b) or MPP-GC synapses (67 ± 6 %, n=6: Figure 3e and f), indicating that L-type Ca2+ channels are not required for these forms of t-LTD.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3a and b.

claim: The L-type Ca2+ channel blocker nimodipine (10 µM) did not impede t-LTD induction at MPP-GC synapses (67 ± 6 %, n=6).
source: This channel blocker did not impede t-LTD induction at LPP-GC (79 ± 4 %, n=6: Figure 3a and b) or MPP-GC synapses (67 ± 6 %, n=6: Figure 3e and f), indicating that L-type Ca2+ channels are not required for these forms of t-LTD.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3e and f.

claim: L-type Ca2+ channels are not required for t-LTD at LPP-GC and MPP-GC synapses.
source: This channel blocker did not impede t-LTD induction at LPP-GC (79 ± 4 %, n=6: Figure 3a and b) or MPP-GC synapses (67 ± 6 %, n=6: Figure 3e and f), indicating that L-type Ca2+ channels are not required for these forms of t-LTD.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of nimodipine on t-LTD.

claim: t-LTD was prevented at LPP-GC synapses when 10 µM thapsigargin was present in the superfusion fluid (108 ± 16%, n=6).
source: Indeed, t-LTD was prevented at both LPP-GC and MPP-GC synapses when 10 µM thapsigargin (a drug that avoids refilling of intracellular Ca2+ stores after Ca2+ depletion, Singh et al., 2021) was present in the superfusion fluid (LPP-GC synapses 108 ± 16%, n=6; MPP-GC synapses108 ± 6 %, n=6),.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3a and b, and a citation to previous work on thapsigargin.

claim: t-LTD was prevented at MPP-GC synapses when 10 µM thapsigargin was present in the superfusion fluid (108 ± 6 %, n=6).
source: Indeed, t-LTD was prevented at both LPP-GC and MPP-GC synapses when 10 µM thapsigargin (a drug that avoids refilling of intracellular Ca2+ stores after Ca2+ depletion, Singh et al., 2021) was present in the superfusion fluid (LPP-GC synapses 108 ± 16%, n=6; MPP-GC synapses108 ± 6 %, n=6),.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3e and f, and a citation to previous work on thapsigargin.

claim: t-LTD was prevented at LPP-GC synapses when thapsigargin (1–10 µM) was loaded into the postsynaptic neuron (107 ± 7%, n=15).
source: A similar effect was witnessed when thapsigargin (1–10 µM) was loaded into the postsynaptic neuron (LPP-GC synapses 107 ± 7%, n=15; MPP-GC synapses 98 ± 4%, n=13) relative to untreated interleaved controls (LPP-GC synapses 65 ± 5%, n=11; MPP-GC synapses 63±6, n=11: Figure 3a, b, e and f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3a and b.

claim: t-LTD was prevented at MPP-GC synapses when thapsigargin (1–10 µM) was loaded into the postsynaptic neuron (98 ± 4%, n=13).
source: A similar effect was witnessed when thapsigargin (1–10 µM) was loaded into the postsynaptic neuron (LPP-GC synapses 107 ± 7%, n=15; MPP-GC synapses 98 ± 4%, n=13) relative to untreated interleaved controls (LPP-GC synapses 65 ± 5%, n=11; MPP-GC synapses 63±6, n=11: Figure 3a, b, e and f).
